claims.text: A hybrid DFT and machine-learning force-field approach can independently and accurately predict lattice and electronic thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed approach will improve predictive accuracy by roughly 20–30% relative to earlier models.
The target material is defect-free, single-phase bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
Approximately 1 wt.% oxygen represents a low or controlled impurity level suitable for the high-temperature application of the model.
Electronic transport will be computed from DFT-derived electronic structure and scattering mechanisms.
Machine-learning-enhanced phonon simulations can capture anharmonicity and disorder without assuming a perfectly periodic lattice.
The approach is applicable from 200 K to 1200 K.
HfNbTaTiZr contains inherent atomic-scale lattice distortions and chemical disorder.
Atomic-size differences in high-entropy solid solutions displace atoms from ideal lattice sites.
Lattice distortions affect phonon scattering, while chemical disorder affects electronic scattering.
Separating electron and phonon transport prevents an averaging error caused by earlier approaches conflating the two contributions.
Physically distinct electronic and phonon simulations will produce more accurate conductivity predictions.
The predicted electronic and lattice conductivities will sum to 10–17 W/(K m) for oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr specimens between 300 K and 1200 K.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable and should be reproduced by the model.
Earlier predictive approaches relied on analytical Debye-temperature estimates or simplified DFT models of ideal, defect-free crystals.
Earlier approaches had broader errors and could not separately capture the temperature dependence of electronic and lattice conductivity.
The model is limited to homogeneous samples with low impurity levels and may fail for high defect densities or secondary phases.
Impurity content, microstructural defects, and limited high-temperature data make the exact accuracy gain uncertain.
Electronic conductivity can be estimated from resistivity using the Wiedemann–Franz law, while lattice conductivity can be inferred from phonon lifetime spectra and specific heat.
The hypothesis is falsified if predicted electronic and lattice conductivities fail to sum to measured total conductivity within ±30%, or if the specified temperature trends are absent.

contradictions.description: The stated applicability and experimental range begins at 200 K, but the prediction and falsification rule require assessment below 200 K.

The material is described as defect-free or near-ideal while also allowing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen; an oxygen-containing specimen is not strictly defect-free unless the meaning of defect-free is narrowed to exclude impurity defects.
